name.text: L7 Q1 Integration tests for infrastructure code

questiontext.text: Why are integration tests on real targets usually worth more than unit tests for infrastructure code?

generalfeedback.text: Infrastructure code mostly orchestrates real systems, so its typical failures appear only when it runs against a target: different distributions ship different packages, paths, and service behavior. Unit tests can be written, but they exercise little of that. Integration tests do not replace linters, which catch a different class of problems before anything runs.

answer.text: Unit tests usually run too slowly to fit into a delivery pipeline for infrastructure code.
Integration tests also check style and conventions, so a separate linter is no longer needed.
Unit tests cannot be written for infrastructure code in any of the common tools.
Most failures appear only when code meets a real system and its packages and services.

questiontext.text: What forms the interface of a reusable infrastructure module?

generalfeedback.text: A module's published parameters and their defaults are how users interact with it: defaults give a working result, and overridable inputs act as extension points. The internal resources and file layout are implementation details that callers should not need to edit or copy. Commit history explains changes but is not the interface.

answer.text: The full set of resources it creates, which callers edit directly when they need changes
The input parameters it publishes, with defaults, that callers set to adjust its behavior
The folder layout of its source files, which callers copy into their own projects
The commit history of its repository, which callers usually read to learn how to use it

questiontext.text: An automation tool already refuses to run a definition with invalid syntax. What does adding a linter contribute?

generalfeedback.text: The tool's own parser already rejects invalid syntax. A linter applies further rules to code that is syntactically valid, catching risky constructs, convention violations, deprecated usage, or ambiguous values such as a number that some parsers read as a string. It is a static check and does not replace running the code on real targets.

answer.text: It replaces integration tests, since a definition that passes linting will behave correctly on real targets.
It runs the definition against a temporary machine and reports which resources failed to start.
It flags valid code that is risky or breaks agreed rules, such as a value parsed as an unexpected type.
It can repeat the tool's syntax check earlier, but it usually reports nothing the tool would accept.

name.text: L7 Q4 Modules as maintained products

questiontext.text: A team plans to extract repeated infrastructure code into a module that other teams will use. Which view is the most sound?

generalfeedback.text: A shared module is a software product: good modules need tests, documentation, examples, a release process, and ongoing effort. That cost is justified as infrastructure complexity and the number of teams grow, because modules also make delegation and knowledge transfer easier. Small setups may not need modules, and modules are also useful inside one organization.

answer.text: A shared module is a product needing tests, docs and releases; it pays off as complexity and teams grow.
A module is mainly a way to shorten files, so it needs no separate testing once the original code worked.
Every project should start with modules, because modules have no maintenance cost compared with plain code.
Modules mostly pay off for code published to public registries, much less for structure inside one company.

name.text: L7 Q5 Order of pipeline checks

questiontext.text: A delivery pipeline for infrastructure code runs linting, policy checks, smoke tests, a staging deployment with integration tests, and then production. Why are the static checks placed first?

generalfeedback.text: Linting and policy checks are fast and need no infrastructure, so placing them first gives quick feedback and stops obvious problems before costly stages create resources. They cannot replace deployment and integration tests, which find problems that only appear on real targets. Each stage still runs its own checks.

answer.text: They catch many problems in seconds, before slower stages spend time or create real resources.
They can find every problem a staging deployment would find, so later stages rarely fail.
Production approval usually depends on how many lint warnings were fixed, more than on test results.
Passing them first lets the later stages skip their own checks and finish the release faster.

name.text: L7 Q6 Assessing a third-party module

questiontext.text: A team finds a public module that does what it needs. Which assessment should come before depending on it?

generalfeedback.text: Signs of a healthy module include recent releases, active issue and security fixing, an evolving interface, and good documentation and examples. If a module looks inactive, its code can still be insourced, adapted, and maintained by the team. Download counts mostly reflect how widely the underlying software is used, not that the module was tested on your platforms; the number of parameters is not a quality measure either.

answer.text: Prefer the module with the most parameters, since a larger interface usually signals higher quality.
Use it if its download count is high, because popularity shows it was tested on your platforms.
Check recent releases, issue fixes, and docs; if it looks inactive, consider insourcing a copy.
Avoid public modules entirely, because code written by outsiders cannot be reviewed or adapted.

questiontext.text: A team wants to manage a new cloud service with code and also standardize how other teams use it. Which split of responsibilities between provider and module fits best?

generalfeedback.text: A provider, or a library of tasks, is the integration layer that turns definitions into API calls for a platform. A module sits one level higher: it combines those resources with the organization's choices into a reusable unit with an interface. Conventions belong in the module, not in the provider.

answer.text: Write a module that calls the service's API directly, and use a provider only to store shared default values.
Use a provider for the service's API, and build a module that combines its resources into a reusable unit.
Ask the cloud vendor for a module, since providers are usually written by each team for its own project.
Treat provider and module as two names for the same layer, so either one can hold the team's conventions.

questiontext.text: A security team wants every infrastructure project to tag resources with their environment and to stay below an agreed instance size. The code is syntactically valid and passes linting. Which approach fits best?

generalfeedback.text: Rules such as required tags, size limits, or approved providers are valid code from the tool's and linter's point of view, so they need a policy engine. Defining them once as policy as code lets the same organization-wide rules run automatically in every project's pipeline and block a release that violates them. Comments and reviewer memory are not enforced, and monitoring catches the problem only after it has reached production.

answer.text: Rely on reviewers to remember the rules, since automated checks can only find syntax errors.
Add the rules as comments in each module, so users can read them before applying changes.
Wait for monitoring to report oversized or untagged resources after they reach production.
Define the rules once as policies and check them in every project's pipeline before release.

name.text: L7 Q9 Adopting a breaking module release

questiontext.text: Staging and production both use version 1.8.2 of a shared network module. Version 2.0.0 adds a feature the team needs and renames some inputs. How should the consuming team adopt it?

generalfeedback.text: A major version signals breaking changes, so the team should pin the new exact version and adapt its inputs. The change should then move through a staged pipeline: automated lint and policy checks, a lower environment such as staging, tests and monitoring, and only then production. Applying to production first, assuming a major release is safe, or changing released code without a new version all remove the predictability that versioning provides.

answer.text: Point both environments at the latest release, apply to production first since it needs the feature most, then fix staging.
Edit the 1.8.2 code in place to add the feature, keeping the version number so no one has to update references.
Switch to 2.0.0 everywhere at once; semantic versioning guarantees a major release will apply cleanly.
Pin 2.0.0, update the renamed inputs, run lint and policy checks, apply to staging, test and monitor, then production.

name.text: L7 Q10 Testing a module across platforms

questiontext.text: An internal configuration module must support the company's Ubuntu and Rocky Linux servers, which start from company-prepared base images. Its only tests are unit tests that run on a laptop. Which testing plan fits best?

generalfeedback.text: Unit tests add little for infrastructure code because the behavior that breaks depends on the real target: package names, defaults, and libraries differ between distributions. Integration tests should run automatically in the pipeline on disposable containers or VMs built from images that match the organization's real baselines, one per supported platform. Testing every possible platform is costly and unnecessary for an internal module, and production servers should not serve as test targets.

answer.text: Add more unit tests until coverage is complete, since they are fast and need no real machines.
In the pipeline, run it on disposable containers or VMs from images like the company's, for each OS.
Test on as many operating systems and clouds as possible first, since the module may be used elsewhere.
Run it once by hand on a production server for each OS, and keep that server as the reference test target.
